intro: Julius Caesar (Shakespeare): leadership, persuasion and responsibility: the big ideas, key words and examples on one sheet. Keep it in your book and use it to revise (cover, write, check).

panels.title: Big questions
points: What makes someone worthy of leading others?
How does the way we write show the quality of our thinking?
How can words lead people to do wrong?
Why are some people so easily persuaded?

panels.title: Islamic foundation
panels.text: Islam teaches that leadership is a trust (amanah, أَمَانَة), not a prize. Allah commands that trusts be given to those worthy of them and that people judge with justice (an-Nisa 4:58), and praises believers whose affairs are settled by consultation (shura) among themselves (ash-Shura 42:38). We read Julius Caesar asking: who is worthy to lead?

panels.title: Julius Caesar: Rome, leadership and Shakespeare's purpose
points: Queen Elizabeth I was old with no heir
People feared civil war over the throne
A play about a power struggle felt urgent
Shakespeare asks: what happens when order breaks?

panels.title: Non-fiction: what makes a great leader?
points: Opens by challenging a common belief
Signposts: 'The first... The second... The third'
An anecdote (the captain) makes it concrete
Short final sentence for emphasis

panels.title: Grammar: formal academic register for literary analysis
points: Third person: 'Shakespeare presents'
Analytical verbs: suggests, conveys, implies
Tentative language: perhaps, may, could
Nominalisation: 'Caesar's ambition' not 'Caesar wants'

panels.title: Act 1: Caesar, the soothsayer and the refused crown; weekly retrieval and DIRT
points: The soothsayer warns: 'Beware the ides of March'
Caesar dismisses him: 'He is a dreamer'
Antony offers Caesar a crown three times
Caesar refuses, but the crowd cheers

panels.title: Cassius and the art of persuasion (Act 1 scene 2)
points: Cassius says the fault is 'in ourselves', not the stars
Rejects fate: people choose their own position
Flatters with 'dear'
Pushes Brutus to act

panels.title: Non-fiction: the psychology of persuasion
points: Ethos: reminds Brutus of his noble ancestor
Pathos: Caesar as a giant, Romans as 'petty men'
Logos: 'Why should that name be sounded more than yours?'
Danger: true tools, misleading purpose

panels.title: Grammar: rhetorical questions, repetition and parallelism
points: identify the three devices in speeches
write a sentence using parallelism
use all three in a short persuasive paragraph

panels.title: Brutus's dilemma: loyalty or duty? (Act 2 scene 1)
points: Brutus cannot sleep
Admits Caesar has done nothing wrong yet
Fears what power might make him
Decides: 'It must be by his death'

panels.title: Non-fiction and grammar: ethical leadership and subordinate clauses
points: identify main and subordinate clauses
use 'although', 'because' and 'unless' to build complex sentences
write a short argument about loyalty and duty using complex sentences

panels.title: How does Shakespeare present the Roman crowd in Act 1 scene 1?
points: Point: the crowd is fickle and easily led.
Evidence: 'You blocks, you stones, you worse than senseless things!'
Technique: list of insults (metaphor)
Zoom in: 'blocks' suggests they do not think
Answer: A PETZAAL paragraph on the fickle crowd.

panels.title: Rewrite: 'I think Caesar is big-headed because he says stuff about himself.'
points: Remove 'I think': use 'It could be argued that'
Upgrade 'big-headed' to 'arrogant'
Replace 'says stuff' with a precise method
Add an analytical verb
Answer: It could be argued that Shakespeare presents Caesar as arrogant: his habit of referring to himself in the third person implies that he sees himself as larger than an ordinary man.

panels.title: Persuade pupils to read every day.
points: Rhetorical question: 'What if ten minutes a day could change your future?'
Parallelism: 'Reading builds your words, sharpens your mind and widens your world.'
Repetition: 'Read today. Read tomorrow. Read always.'
Answer: What if ten minutes a day could change your future? Reading builds your words, sharpens your mind and widens your world. Read today. Read tomorrow. Read always.

panels.title: Write about Brutus using three conjunctions.
points: Concession: 'Although Brutus loves Caesar, he joins the plot.'
Reason: 'He acts because he fears tyranny.'
Condition: 'Unless Caesar is stopped, Brutus believes Rome will fall.'
Comma rule: comma after a fronted subordinate clause
Answer: Although Brutus loves Caesar, he joins the plot because he fears tyranny; unless Caesar is stopped, he believes, Rome will lose its freedom.
